name: Salvador Puig Antich
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Puig Antich was executed at age 25 in 1974 for killing a police officer during a shootout; his notability derives from martyrdom under the Franco regime, not from a positive achievement or success milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Barcelona in 1948, Puig Antich joined the militant Iberian Liberation Movement (MIL) in the early 1970s and participated in armed bank robberies to fund anti-Franco activities. He was captured in September 1973 after a shootout that killed a police officer and was executed by garrote in March 1974 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Born into a Catalan family in Barcelona; his four sisters later campaigned for posthumous review of his case. Further family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Moshe Safdie
milestone_by_age_26: At age 25 in 1963-64, Safdie was invited by his thesis advisor Sandy van Ginkel to adapt his McGill undergraduate thesis on modular housing as the central feature of Expo 67 (Habitat 67), and established his own firm in 1964 to realize the project.
early_history_summary: Born in Haifa in 1938, Safdie emigrated to Montreal with his family at age 15 after his father's textile business was hurt by import restrictions. He enrolled in McGill's architecture program at 17, developed an innovative modular housing thesis, and after apprenticing with Louis Kahn was tapped to realize his thesis as Habitat 67 for Expo 67.
family_context_summary: Born to a Syrian Jewish family in Haifa; father ran a textile business that struggled under Israeli import restrictions, prompting the family's emigration to Montreal in 1953 when Safdie was 15.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was in the textile business, not directly related to architecture; no evidence of parental domain expertise in architecture.
primary_early_advantage_tags: McGill architecture, Louis Kahn apprenticeship, van Ginkel mentorship, Expo 67 platform
evidence_summary: Safdie's path to Habitat 67 was catalyzed by elite institutional access (McGill University), sustained mentorship (thesis advisor van Ginkel who connected him to Expo 67, apprenticeship with Louis Kahn), and a structural wave (Montreal's World's Fair). His family's middle-class background and emigration to Montreal provided the geographic proximity to McGill and Expo 67. The modular housing thesis demonstrated genuine technical depth and innovation, but the critical accelerator was van Ginkel's invitation to realize it at a World's Fair.
starting_point: Born to a Syrian Jewish family in Haifa, Mandatory Palestine; father ran a textile business that struggled under import restrictions, prompting the family's emigration to Montreal in 1953 when Safdie was 15.
current_position: Founder and principal of Safdie Architects; continues to design major projects worldwide including Marina Bay Sands and Jewel Changi Airport; based in Boston, MA.

trajectory.event: Graduated from McGill University with a degree in architecture, developing his thesis on modular housing.
Returned to Montreal and established his own firm to realize Habitat 67 for Expo 67, adapting his undergraduate thesis.
Habitat 67 opened as the central feature of Expo 67, becoming an iconic work of modern architecture.
Began teaching at Harvard University's Graduate School of Design.
Marina Bay Sands in Singapore opened, becoming one of his most recognized projects worldwide.
Jewel Changi Airport in Singapore opened, further cementing his legacy as a world-renowned architect.

name: Mino De Rossi
milestone_by_age_26: At age 19 in 1950, De Rossi broke the World Hour Record for amateurs (42.481 km); at age 20 in 1951, he won the UCI Amateur Track World Championships individual pursuit; at age 21 in 1952, he won Olympic gold in the men's 4000m team pursuit at Helsinki.
early_history_summary: Born in Arquata Scrivia, Italy in 1931, De Rossi emerged as a talented amateur track cyclist in the Italian cycling system. He broke the World Hour Record for amateurs at 19, won the world championship individual pursuit at 20, and claimed Olympic gold in team pursuit at 21 before turning professional with the Bianchi team.
family_context_summary: Born in Arquata Scrivia, Piedmont, Italy. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Italian cycling tradition, amateur track system, team pursuit, post-war cycling boom
evidence_summary: De Rossi benefited from Italy's deep cycling tradition and the amateur track cycling pipeline that produced world-class riders in the post-war era. His World Hour Record at 19 and world championship at 20 demonstrate exceptional physical talent and early specialization. The team pursuit Olympic gold relied on complementary teammates. Limited information is available about his family background or specific coaching relationships.
starting_point: Born in Arquata Scrivia, Italy; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on January 7, 2022 at age 90 in Genoa; after retiring from professional cycling in 1967, worked as a Michelin tire salesman and helped organize amateur cycling events.

trajectory.event: Broke the World Hour Record for amateurs, setting it at 42.481 km.
Won the UCI Amateur Track World Championships individual pursuit.
Won Olympic gold medal in men's 4000m team pursuit at the Helsinki Olympics.
Turned professional with the Bianchi team alongside Fausto Coppi.
Won the Six Days of Buenos Aires track cycling event.
Retired from professional cycling after a career spanning road and track disciplines.
Died on January 7, 2022, in Genoa, Italy.

name: Bobby Hull
milestone_by_age_26: At age 18 in 1957, Hull made his NHL debut with the Chicago Black Hawks and was Calder Trophy runner-up; at age 21 in 1960, he won the Art Ross Trophy as NHL scoring champion (39 goals, 81 points) and was named to the NHL First All-Star Team.
early_history_summary: Born in Point Anne, Ontario in 1939 to a cement company foreman, Hull grew up on a farm near Belleville and showed exceptional hockey talent from a young age. He played junior B hockey at 15, progressed through the OHA, and joined the Chicago Black Hawks at 18, becoming the league's top scorer by 21.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Point Anne, Ontario; father Robert Edward Hull was a cement company foreman. Hull grew up on a farm near Belleville, Ontario.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental hockey expertise or industry connections; father was a cement company foreman.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Canadian hockey culture, OHA junior pipeline, early NHL entry, exceptional physical talent
evidence_summary: Hull's path was defined by exceptional raw physical talent recognized early—he played junior hockey at 15 and was in the NHL at 18 without looking out of place. The OHA junior system and Chicago Black Hawks organization provided the elite performance pipeline. Growing up in rural Ontario immersed him in Canadian hockey culture. His working-class farm background offered no financial platform but did provide direct domain exposure to hockey from childhood. His physical edge (speed and shot power) was exceptional and changed how the game was played.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Point Anne, Ontario; father was a cement company foreman, grew up on a farm near Belleville.
current_position: Died on January 30, 2023 at age 84 in Wheaton, Illinois; retired as one of the greatest NHL players of all time, inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 1983.

trajectory.event: Made NHL debut with the Chicago Black Hawks, finishing second in Calder Trophy voting with 47 points.
Won the Art Ross Trophy as NHL scoring champion with 39 goals and 81 points, named to First All-Star Team.
Led the Chicago Black Hawks to their first Stanley Cup victory in 23 years.
Scored 50 goals in a season, tying Maurice Richard's all-time record.
Scored 54 goals and won his second Hart Trophy as NHL MVP.
Signed a $1 million contract to join the Winnipeg Jets in the World Hockey Association.
Inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame.
Died on January 30, 2023, in Wheaton, Illinois.

name: Michael York
milestone_by_age_26: At age 23 in 1965, York was selected by Laurence Olivier for the National Theatre Company and cast by Franco Zeffirelli in Much Ado About Nothing; at age 25 in 1967, he made his film debut as Lucentio in Zeffirelli's The Taming of the Shrew and appeared in the acclaimed BBC miniseries The Forsyte Saga.
early_history_summary: Born in Fulmer, Buckinghamshire in 1942 to a Marks & Spencer executive and a musician, York began acting as a teenager in community theatre and the National Youth Theatre. He studied English at Oxford, acted with the Oxford University Dramatic Society, then joined the Dundee Repertory Theatre and was selected for Olivier's National Theatre Company at 23.
family_context_summary: Born to a middle-class family in Fulmer, Buckinghamshire; father Joseph Gwynne Johnson was a Welsh ex-Royal Artillery officer turned Marks & Spencer executive; mother Florence Edith May Chown was a musician.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a businessman (Marks & Spencer executive) and mother was a musician; no direct family domain expertise in acting, though middle-class cultural capital supported access to theatre and Oxford.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Oxford University, National Youth Theatre, Olivier's National Theatre, Zeffirelli mentorship, London theatre ecosystem
evidence_summary: York's career was accelerated by elite institutional access: the National Youth Theatre as a teenager, Oxford University's Dramatic Society, and crucially, selection by Laurence Olivier for the National Theatre Company at 23. Olivier and Zeffirelli served as high-quality mentors who directly cast him in stage and film roles. His middle-class background (father a Marks & Spencer executive) provided the cultural and financial platform for Oxford and London theatre access. The 1960s British film and theatre renaissance provided a structural wave.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Fulmer, Buckinghamshire; father was a Welsh ex-Royal Artillery officer turned Marks & Spencer executive, mother was a musician.
current_position: Continues acting and voice work; resides in California; was treated for amyloidosis in 2013 and later recovered following stem cell treatment.

trajectory.event: Made West End debut with a small part in a production of Hamlet.
Graduated from Oxford University and joined the Dundee Repertory Theatre.
Joined Laurence Olivier's National Theatre Company, cast by Franco Zeffirelli in Much Ado About Nothing.
Made film debut as Lucentio in Zeffirelli's The Taming of the Shrew and appeared in the BBC's The Forsyte Saga.
Played Tybalt in Zeffirelli's Romeo and Juliet, achieving international breakthrough.
Starred as Brian Roberts in the Academy Award-winning film Cabaret.
Played D'Artagnan in The Three Musketeers and its sequels.

name: Antoaneta Stefanova
milestone_by_age_26: At age 10 in 1989, won the Girls U10 World Youth Chess Championship; at age 13 in 1992, debuted at the Chess Olympiad; at age 16 in 1995, won the Bulgarian women's championship; at age 23 in 2002, became European Women's Champion and was awarded the GM title (9th woman ever); at age 25 in 2004, won the Women's World Chess Championship.
early_history_summary: Born in Sofia, Bulgaria in 1979, Stefanova learned chess from her father at age four. She was a prodigy—winning Sofia's women's championship at seven, the world U10 title at ten, and debuting at the Chess Olympiad at 13. She won the Bulgarian women's championship at 16, became European champion and a grandmaster at 23, and claimed the Women's World Championship at 25.
family_context_summary: Born in Sofia, Bulgaria; father Andon Stefanov was a designing artist who taught her chess at age four, believing chess improves spatial imagination.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a designing artist (not a chess professional) who introduced chess as a cognitive development tool; his sustained early teaching was catalytic despite not being a domain expert.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Father as chess teacher, early prodigy, Bulgarian chess tradition, sustained individualized training from age 4
evidence_summary: Stefanova's trajectory was defined by extraordinarily early specialization—chess from age four, taught by her father who provided sustained individualized mentorship. She demonstrated genuine prodigy-level ability (Sofia women's champion at seven, world U10 champion at ten). Bulgaria's strong chess tradition and the Chess Olympiad pipeline provided the elite ecosystem. Her progression to grandmaster (9th woman ever) and Women's World Champion by 25 reflects exceptional skill depth built on 20+ years of sustained practice. No financial platform was documented.
starting_point: Born in Sofia, Bulgaria; father was a designing artist who taught her chess at age four, believing it improves spatial imagination.
current_position: Active chess grandmaster and politician; led Bulgaria to victory at the European women's team championship in 2024; was her party's Prime Ministerial candidate in Bulgaria.

trajectory.event: Won the Girls U10 section at the World Youth Chess Festival in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico.
Debuted at the Chess Olympiad in Manila; became European U14 girls' champion the same year.
Won the Bulgarian women's chess championship.
Won the European Individual Women's Championship and was awarded the grandmaster title, becoming the ninth woman to reach GM rank.
Won the Women's World Chess Championship in Elista, becoming the 10th women's world champion.
Won the World Rapid Chess Championship and reached the final of the Women's World Championship.
Led Bulgaria to victory at the European women's team chess championship.

name: Nico Hülkenberg
milestone_by_age_26: At age 18 in 2005, won the Formula BMW ADAC championship; at age 19-20 in 2006-07, won the A1 Grand Prix series for Germany with nine victories; at age 21 in 2008, won the Formula 3 Euro Series; at age 22 in 2009, won the GP2 Series championship in his rookie season; at age 22-23 in 2010, made F1 debut with Williams and claimed pole position at the Brazilian Grand Prix.
early_history_summary: Born in Emmerich am Rhein, Germany in 1987, Hülkenberg began karting at age 10, winning German junior karting titles by 15. He progressed through Formula BMW (champion at 18), A1 Grand Prix (champion at 19-20), Formula 3 Euro Series (champion at 21), and GP2 (champion at 22), reaching Formula One in 2010 with Williams.
family_context_summary: Born and raised in Emmerich am Rhein, Germany. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Karting from age 10, Willi Weber management, German motorsport boom, junior formula progression
evidence_summary: Hülkenberg's path was defined by early and systematic progression through junior racing categories, starting with karting at 10. The German motorsport boom of the Schumacher era created a fertile ecosystem. Being spotted by Willi Weber (Schumacher's manager) provided management and mentorship. His dominance in A1 Grand Prix (nine wins) and GP2 championship in his rookie season demonstrated exceptional driving skill. No family financial platform or domain expertise was documented, suggesting his progression was largely merit-based through the junior formula pipeline.
starting_point: Born and raised in Emmerich am Rhein, Germany; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Formula One driver for Stake F1 Team (Sauber), transitioning to Audi in 2026; achieved his maiden F1 podium at the 2025 British Grand Prix.

trajectory.event: Won the German Junior Karting Championship.
Won the Formula BMW ADAC championship in his rookie season.
Dominated the A1 Grand Prix series, winning nine races to secure the championship for Team Germany.
Won the Formula 3 Euro Series championship with ART.

name: Vladimir Smirnov
milestone_by_age_26: At age 18 in 1982, made FIS World Cup debut; at age 22 in 1986, secured first World Cup victory; at age 23 in 1987, won World Championship silver in relay; at age 23 in 1988, won three Olympic medals at Calgary (silver 30km, silver relay, bronze 15km); at age 25 in 1989, won his first World Championship gold in 30km.
early_history_summary: Born in Shchuchinsk, Kazakh SSR in 1964 to Russian parents, Smirnov started cross-country skiing at age 11. He trained within the Soviet Armed Forces sports society in Alma-Ata, made his World Cup debut at 18, and rose to international prominence with his first World Cup victory at 22 and three Olympic medals at the 1988 Calgary Games at 23.
family_context_summary: Born to Russian parents in Shchuchinsk, Kazakh SSR. Further family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet Armed Forces sports society, skiing from age 11, Kazakhstan winter sports, systematic coaching
evidence_summary: Smirnov's development was shaped by the Soviet sports system, which provided systematic training through the Armed Forces sports society in Alma-Ata. Starting skiing at 11 in Kazakhstan gave him early domain exposure, and the Soviet pipeline concentrated opportunity through coaching and facilities. His World Cup debut at 18 and first victory at 22 demonstrate strong physical talent and early specialization. No family financial platform or domain expertise was documented. His Olympic success at 23 validated the pipeline's effectiveness.
starting_point: Born to Russian parents in Shchuchinsk, Kazakh SSR; family background beyond this not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Vice president of the International Biathlon Union (IBU); former IOC member for Kazakhstan; resides in Sweden.

Won three gold medals at the World Championships in Thunder Bay.
